title: VC Valuation: Pre-Money to Exit
description: Master the mechanics of VC valuation including pre/post-money, revenue multiples, and return-driven pricing.

interactions.prompt: A VC invests $5M at a $15M pre-money valuation. What percentage of the company do they own?

options.text: 25% — $5M of $20M post-money
33% — $5M of $15M pre-money
20% — $5M of $25M post-money
30% — blended pre and post calculation

interactions.teachingPreamble: Pre-money valuation is what the company is worth before new investment; post-money equals pre-money plus the investment amount. Ownership percentage is always calculated against post-money: Investment ÷ Post-Money = Ownership %. For example, when Stripe raised its Series A, investors' stakes were determined by dividing their check size by the post-money valuation.

interactions.prompt: A Series B SaaS company shows: ARR $12M growing 110% YoY, gross margin 78%, net revenue retention 135%, burn multiple 1.8x. Comparable public SaaS companies at similar growth trade at 20-30x ARR. What's the most critical signal for justifying the upper end of that range?

options.text: 78% gross margin is strong but standard for SaaS
135% NRR signals compounding revenue without new customers
110% growth alone justifies premium multiples
1.8x burn multiple shows capital efficiency

chartData.title: Series B Company Metrics vs. SaaS Benchmarks

interactions.prompt: A VC targets 3x on a $10M Series B and expects exit in 5 years at 10x revenue. The startup currently has $8M ARR growing 60% YoY. Using the VC method, which factor most directly sets the required pre-money valuation today?

options.text: Current ARR of $8M determines today's value
Projected exit value discounted by the target return multiple
Comparable company multiples applied to current revenue
TAM penetration rate at time of exit

interactions.teachingPreamble: The VC method works backward from exit. You estimate the terminal value at exit (e.g., projected revenue × exit multiple), then divide by the target return multiple to get the post-money valuation today. This is fundamentally different from DCF—VCs price rounds based on what return they need, not a cost-of-capital discount rate. Sequoia famously uses variants of this approach to back into acceptable entry prices.

interactions.prompt: In the VC method, if a startup's projected exit value is $600M and the fund requires a 10x return, the maximum ____ valuation the VC should pay is $60M.

options.text: Pre-money
Post-money
Enterprise
Liquidation

interactions.prompt: You're leading a Series A for a fintech doing $4M ARR (growing 150% YoY) with 18 months of runway. Founder wants $80M pre-money (20x ARR). A competitor term sheet offers $60M pre-money. Do you match, counter, or walk?

options.text: Match at $80M — 150% growth justifies premium, losing deal is worse
Counter at $65M — slight premium over competitor, preserves return math
Walk away — $80M pre-money destroys Series B step-up economics
Offer $80M but with 2x liquidation preference to protect downside

interactions.prompt: A marketplace startup claims $2B TAM. Their current GMV is $50M with a 15% take rate ($7.5M net revenue). An investor models 5% TAM penetration at maturity. What's the flaw in using this TAM figure to back into a valuation?

options.text: TAM should use GMV not net revenue as the base
5% penetration is unrealistically conservative for venture returns
TAM is likely top-down and doesn't reflect serviceable obtainable market
Take rate will increase so $7.5M understates current revenue

interactions.teachingPreamble: TAM-based valuation sizes the opportunity ceiling, but investors frequently confuse Total Addressable Market with Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM). A $2B TAM might yield only a $200M SOM after filtering for geography, customer segment, and competitive dynamics. Uber's early pitch cited a $4B global taxi market—their actual addressable opportunity was far larger because they redefined the market, illustrating how TAM framing can mislead in both directions.

interactions.prompt: Rank these inputs by their impact on a growth-stage SaaS company's valuation multiple, from MOST to LEAST impactful: (a) Gross margin improvement from 72% to 80%, (b) Revenue growth acceleration from 80% to 130% YoY, (c) TAM expansion from $5B to $8B, (d) Net revenue retention improvement from 110% to 140%.

options.text: Gross margin: 72% → 80%
Revenue growth: 80% → 130% YoY
TAM expansion: $5B → $8B
Net revenue retention: 110% → 140%

interactions.prompt: The macro environment shifts: interest rates jump 300bps and public SaaS multiples compress from 25x to 12x ARR. Your portfolio company was valued at $200M post-money (25x on $8M ARR) just 9 months ago and now needs to raise a Series C. What's your best move?

options.text: Raise a flat round at $200M to avoid a down round signal
Accept a down round at 15x ARR to get clean capital in
Extend runway via bridge note, delay pricing until multiples recover
Push for 20x ARR with heavy structured terms and preferences

interactions.priorContext: Previously, the company raised at 25x ARR in a favorable market. Now public SaaS multiples have compressed by over 50% due to a 300bps rate hike, fundamentally changing the comparable valuation framework and making the prior round's pricing look aggressive.
